title: Getting started
subtitle: Your first steps in Swiss German
description: Find out what Swiss German is, how it's spoken and written, and how to approach learning it, before you learn your first words.

expectations.title: Understand how Swiss German relates to Standard German
Know how Swiss German is spoken and written
Know how to approach learning it

sections.title: What is Swiss German?
sections.description: What Swiss German is, and where it's spoken.

rules.title: Two kinds of German
rules.takeaway: In Switzerland, people generally speak Swiss German in everyday life but use Swiss Standard German for most formal writing.
rules.theory: In Switzerland, you'll meet two forms of German.

items.text: The Alemannic dialects of German-speaking Switzerland, with their own words, sounds and sentence structure. Spoken in everyday life, with family, friends and colleagues.
Switzerland's version of Standard German (often called Hochdeutsch), almost the same as in Germany. Used mainly in writing, at school and in formal settings.

rules.title: One language, many dialects
rules.theory:
Swiss German consists of different regional dialects. The way people speak varies depending on where they come from. The main dialect regions include Zürich, Bern, Basel and Eastern Switzerland.

Some words and expressions are pronounced differently across regions.
rules.note: Swiss German has no standardised spelling. These examples show regional variations; the differences are often even more noticeable in pronunciation.
rules.takeaway: You don't need to learn every dialect. Learn yours well, and you'll soon understand the others too: Swiss people from different regions understand each other easily.

sections.title: How to learn Swiss German
sections.description: How Swiss German is spoken and written, and how it goes with Standard German.

rules.title: Start with your ears
rules.theory: Swiss German is primarily a spoken language, and for many non-native speakers, pronunciation is one of the biggest challenges. The best way to start is to get familiar with the sounds that are typical of Swiss German.

points.heading: How to start: train your ear
items: Get used to hearing them in short sentences.

rules.takeaway: The more you listen, the easier it becomes to recognise the sounds and say them yourself.

rules.title: Written as it sounds
rules.theory: Swiss German is mainly spoken. When people write it, they often spell words the way they pronounce them. Unlike Swiss Standard German, it has no official spelling rules, so the same word can be written in different ways.

points.heading: Three ways to write “I saw your father yesterday.”

items.term: I ha geschter dy fattr xee
I ha gester di Vater gseh
I ha geschter di Vater gsee

rules.note: (Swiss) Standard German: Ich habe gestern deinen Vater gesehen.
rules.takeaway: Don't let the different spellings confuse you. There's no single correct way to write Swiss German, and it's mostly spoken anyway. You'll get used to the variations as you learn.

rules.title: Swiss German or Standard German?
rules.theory: What should you learn first: Swiss German or Standard German? You can learn one after the other, or just one of them. Many people learn both together, and that's what we recommend: the two share much of their vocabulary and grammar, so each helps with the other.

points.heading: Learning both gives you
items: Standard German for writing, official matters and permits.
Swiss German to follow everyday conversations and join in.
A head start in each, since they share so much.

rules.takeaway: Hoi focuses on Swiss German, the language you'll hear every day. Next to every word and phrase, you also see the Standard German, so you pick it up along the way.
